title: That our desires are augmented by difficulty
paragraphs: There is no reason that does not have its contrary, say the wisest of the philosophers. I was just now ruminating on the excellent saying one of the ancients gives as a reason for the contempt of life: "No good can bring pleasure unless it is one for the loss of which we are prepared beforehand."
"In aequo est dolor amissae rei, et timor amittendae,"
["The grief of losing a thing, and the fear of losing it, are equal." — Seneca, Ep., 98.]

meaning by this that the enjoyment of life cannot be truly pleasant to us if we are in fear of losing it. It might however be said, on the contrary, that we hug and embrace this good so much the more keenly, and with so much greater affection, by how much we see it less secure and fear it being taken from us. For it is plain — as fire burns with greater fury when cold comes to mix with it — that our will is more obstinate by being opposed:
"Si nunquam Danaen habuisset ahenea turris, Non esses, Danae, de Jove facta parens;"
["If a brazen tower had not held Danae, you would not, Danae, have been made a mother by Jove." — Ovid, Amor., ii. 19, 27.]
and there is nothing naturally so contrary to our taste as satiety, which comes from ease; nor anything that so much whets it as rarity and difficulty:
"Omnium rerum voluptas ipso, quo debet fugare, periculo crescit."
["The pleasure of all things grows by the same danger that should deter us from them." — Seneca, De Benef., vii. 9.]
"Galla, nega; satiatur amor, nisi gaudia torquent."
["Galla, refuse me; love is glutted by joys that are not attended with trouble." — Martial, iv. 37.]

To keep love breathing, Lycurgus made a decree that married couples in Lacedaemon should never come together except by stealth, and that to be caught in bed together would be as great a shame as to be caught with others. The difficulty of assignations, the danger of being surprised, the shame of the morning,
"Et languor, et silentium, Et latere petitus imo Spiritus:"
["And languor, and silence, and sighs drawn from deep within." — Horace, Epod., xi. 9.]

these are what give the sauce its piquancy. How many very wantonly pleasant games spring from the most decent and modest language in writings about love? Pleasure itself wants to be heightened by pain; it is much sweeter when it smarts, when it leaves the skin rippled. The courtesan Flora said she never lay with Pompey but that she left him wearing the marks of her teeth.

"Quod petiere, premunt arcte, faciuntque dolorem Corporis, et dentes inlidunt saepe labellis . . . Et stimuli subsunt, qui instigant laedere ad ipsum, Quodcunque est, rabies unde illae germina surgunt."

["What they have sought they press close, causing bodily pain; teeth fix on lips, kisses leave their mark: hidden goads urge them to wound the very part from which that madness rises." — Lucretius, iv. 1077.]

And so it is in everything: difficulty gives all things their value. The people of the March of Ancona more readily make their vows to St James, those of Galicia to Our Lady of Loreto; they make a great fuss at Liège about the baths of Lucca, and in Tuscany about those of Aspa; there are few Romans to be seen in the fencing school at Rome, which is full of Frenchmen. That great Cato also, as much as the rest of us, grew weary of his wife while she was his, and longed for her when she was in another man's possession. I once had to turn an old horse out to pasture, because he was unmanageable when he smelt a mare: ease quickly sated him as to his own, but for strange mares — and the first that passed along his fence — he would fall again to his pressing neighings and his furious heats, as before. Our appetite scorns and passes by what it has in possession, to run after what it does not have:
"Transvolat in medio posita, et fugientia captat."
["He passes over what lies in his path, and chases after what flees from him." — Horace, Sat., i. 2, 108.]
To forbid us anything is to make us have a mind to it:
"Nisi tu servare puellam Incipis, incipiet desinere esse mea:"
["Unless you begin to guard your mistress, she will soon stop being mine." — Ovid, Amor., ii. 19, 47.]
to give it up to us entirely is to breed in us contempt. Want and abundance fall into the same difficulty:
"Tibi quod superest, mihi quod desit, dolet."
["Your superfluities trouble you, and what I lack troubles me." — Terence, Phorm., i. 3, 9.]

Desire and fulfilment afflict us equally. The harshness of mistresses is hard to bear, but ease, to tell the truth, is harder still — since discontent and anger spring from the value we set on the thing desired, and stir love into life, while satiety breeds disgust; it is a blunt, dull, stupid, tired, slothful passion:
"Si qua volet regnare diu, contemnat amantem."
["She who would long retain her power, let her treat her lover with disdain." — Ovid, Amor., ii. 19, 33.]
"Contemnite, amantes: Sic hodie veniet, si qua negavit heri."
["Be scornful, lovers: she who refused you yesterday will come today." — Propertius, ii. 14, 19.]

Why did Poppaea invent the use of a mask to hide the beauties of her face, but to enhance them in the eyes of her lovers? Why have women veiled, even down to the heels, those beauties that everyone wants to show and that everyone wants to see? Why do they cover with so many hindrances, one on top of another, the parts where our desire — and their own — has its principal seat? And to what serve those huge bastion farthingales with which our ladies fortify their hips, but to whet our appetite and to draw us on by removing the goal further from us?
"Et fugit ad salices, et se cupit ante videri."
["She flies to the willows, and yet wants to be seen before she does." — Virgil, Eclog., iii. 65.]
"Interdum tunica duxit operta moram."
["The hidden robe has at times held back love." — Propertius, ii. 15, 6.]

What use is the artifice of this virgin modesty, this grave coldness, this severe look, this professing to be ignorant of things they know better than we, who instruct them in them — but to increase in us the desire to overcome, to control, to trample underfoot at pleasure all this ceremony and all these obstacles? For there is not only pleasure but, on top of that, glory in conquering and corrupting that soft sweetness and childish modesty, and reducing a cold and matronlike gravity to the mercy of our burning desires. It is a glory, they say, to triumph over modesty, chastity, and temperance; and whoever talks ladies out of these qualities betrays both them and himself. We are to believe that their hearts tremble with fright, that the very sound of our words offends the purity of their ears, that they hate us for talking so, and only yield to our pressing by a kind of compulsion. Beauty, all-powerful as it is, has not the means to make itself relished without the help of these little arts. Look at Italy, where there is the most beauty for sale, and the finest, and see how it is forced to have recourse to extrinsic means and other artifices to make itself charming — and yet, in truth, whatever it does, being venal and public, it remains feeble and languishing. So too in virtue itself: of two equal effects, we look upon the one as the finer and worthier in which more trouble and risk have been set before us.

It is an effect of divine Providence to allow the holy Church to be afflicted, as we see her, with so many storms and troubles — by this opposition to rouse pious souls, and to wake them from that drowsy lethargy into which, through so long a tranquillity, they had sunk. If we should set the loss we have suffered, in the number of those who have gone astray, against the benefit we have had in being brought to breathe again, and in having our zeal and strength revived by reason of this opposition, I do not know whether the gain would not overtop the damage.

We thought to tie the nuptial knot of our marriages more firm and fast by taking away all means of dissolving it; but the knot of the will and affection is so much the more slackened and loosened the closer the knot of constraint is drawn. And on the contrary, what kept marriages at Rome so long in honour and inviolate was the liberty everyone had to break them at will. They kept their wives the better because they could part with them if they wished; and, in the full liberty of divorce, five hundred years and more passed before anyone made use of it.
"Quod licet, ingratum est; quod non licet, acrius urit."
["What is allowed, gives no pleasure; what is forbidden, sharpens the appetite." — Ovid, Amor., ii. 19.]

We might bring in here the opinion of an ancient writer on this point: "That executions rather whet than dull the edge of vices; that they do not breed any care of doing well — that being the work of reason and discipline — but only a care not to be caught in doing ill":
"Latius excisae pestis contagia serpunt."
["The plague-sore, once lanced, spreads its contagion all the more." — Rutilius, Itinerar., i. 397.]
I do not know that this is true; but I know by experience that civil government was never reformed by such means; the order and regulation of manners depend on some other expedient.

The Greek histories make mention of the Argippians, neighbours of Scythia, who live without rod or stick for any offence; where not only does no one attempt to attack them, but whoever can flee to them is safe, by reason of their virtue and sanctity of life, and no one dares lay hands on them — and they have applications made to them to settle the disputes that arise between men of other countries. There is a certain nation where the enclosures of the gardens and fields they want to preserve are made only of a string of cotton; and, so fenced, are more firm and secure than by our hedges and ditches.
"Furem signata sollicitant . . . aperta effractarius praeterit."
["Things sealed up tempt the thief; the housebreaker passes by open doors." — Seneca, Epist., 68.]

Perhaps the openness of my house, among other things, has been a means of preserving it from the violence of our civil wars: defence invites attack, and defiance provokes an enemy. I disabled the soldiers' design by stripping the exploit of danger and of all the military glory that usually serves them as pretext and excuse — for whatever is done bravely is always done honourably, in a time when justice is dead. I render the conquest of my house cowardly and base; it is never shut to anyone who knocks; my gate has no other guard than a porter, and he by ancient custom and ceremony — who does not so much serve to defend it as to offer it with more decorum and grace. I have no other guard or sentinel than the stars. A gentleman would play the fool to make a show of defence if he were not really in a condition to defend himself. He who lies open on one side lies open everywhere. Our ancestors did not think of building frontier garrisons. The means of assaulting — without battery or army, I mean — and of surprising our houses, increases every day more and more beyond the means to guard them; men's wits are generally bent that way; in invasion everyone is concerned; in defence, only the rich. Mine was strong for the time when it was built; I have added nothing to it of that kind, and would be afraid that its strength might turn against me; besides which, we have to bear in mind that a time of peace would require it to be dismantled. There is a danger of never being able to retake it, and it would be very hard to hold; for in intestine quarrels, your own man may be of the party you fear, and where religion is the pretext, even one's nearest relations become unreliable, with some colour of justice. The public exchequer will not maintain our domestic garrisons; they would exhaust it. We ourselves do not have the means to do it without ruin — or, what is more inconvenient and harmful, without ruining the people. The condition of my loss would scarcely be worse. As to the rest, you there lose everything; and even your friends would more readily blame your lack of vigilance, your lack of foresight, your ignorance of and indifference to your own affairs, than pity you. That so many garrisoned houses have been undone, while mine remains, makes me apt to believe that they were lost only by being guarded; this gives an enemy both an invitation and a colour of reason; all defence shows the face of war. Let whoever wishes come to me in God's name; but I shall not invite them. This is the retirement I have chosen for my repose from war. I try to withdraw this corner from the public storm, as I also do another corner in my soul. Our war may take whatever forms it likes, multiply and diversify itself into new parties; for my part, I do not stir. Among so many garrisoned houses, I alone of those of my rank, so far as I know, in France, have trusted purely to Heaven for the protection of mine, and have never removed plate, deeds, or hangings. I will neither fear nor save myself by halves. If a full acknowledgment earns the divine favour, it will stay with me to the end; if not, I have still gone on long enough to make my continuance remarkable and worth recording. How? Why, it has been thirty years that I have lived this way.
